course_title: Experimental Methods in Aerospace Engineering I
course_desc: Wind tunnel testing, pressure transducers, strain gauges, and data acquisition systems form the toolkit for this first course in aerospace experimentation. Students plan simple test matrices, calibrate instruments, and propagate measurement uncertainty through calculated results. Emphasis falls on building the habits of careful observation and honest error reporting that later design and research courses assume are already in place.

Weekly experiments introduce the basic apparatus of aerospace testing: a subsonic wind tunnel for airfoil pressure distributions, load frames for beam and column testing, and a shock tube for an introduction to compressible flow. Each session pairs a short apparatus briefing with data collection, and students submit a formal lab report analyzing results against theoretical predictions. The course establishes report format, units discipline, and error estimation used throughout the sequence. Laboratory companion to AERO-1005.

Covers the fundamentals of incompressible aerodynamics: airfoil theory, thin-airfoil and lifting-line approximations, boundary layer behavior, and the sources of lift and drag on wings and bodies. Potential flow solutions, pressure coefficients, and simple panel methods give students hand-calculation tools before any computational treatment. Problem sets connect theory to real airfoil geometries and wing planforms used in general aviation and early jet aircraft.

Numerical methods central to aerospace practice are introduced here: root finding, numerical integration, linear system solvers, and finite-difference approximations to ordinary differential equations, applied to trajectory, structural, and flow problems drawn from the rest of the curriculum. Students write and debug their own short programs rather than relying on packaged solvers, building intuition for where numerical error and instability come from. No prior programming background beyond basic scripting is assumed.

Introduces the finite element method through one-dimensional bar and beam elements before extending to plane stress and plane strain problems in two dimensions. Topics include shape functions, stiffness matrix assembly, boundary condition application, and mesh convergence, worked by hand on small problems before moving to a simple solver. Students leave able to set up and interpret a basic structural finite element model, not just operate a commercial package.

Surveys how an aircraft or spacecraft fits together as an integrated system: propulsion, structures, avionics, and controls, and the trade-offs engineers make when none of these subsystems can be optimized in isolation. Case studies of existing aircraft and small satellites illustrate how requirements flow down from mission need to subsystem specification. A term project has student teams size a simple vehicle concept against a stated mission requirement.

course_title: Introduction to Aerospace Engineering Systems Laboratory
course_desc: Hands-on sessions build small subsystem demonstrations tied to the topics covered in lecture: a servo-actuated control surface, a simple avionics breadboard, and a scale structural mockup instrumented with strain gauges. Students disassemble and measure components, record subsystem performance data, and write short reports connecting bench results to the systems concepts covered that week. Laboratory companion to AERO-1030.

Examines how flows transition from laminar to turbulent and the statistical tools engineers use once that transition happens: Reynolds decomposition, the closure problem, boundary layer turbulence, and simple mixing-length models. Classic experiments and flow visualizations anchor the discussion of eddy structure and energy cascade. The course builds physical intuition for turbulence that later coursework in computational fluid dynamics and propulsion takes for granted.

A broad first look at how airplanes fly and are designed, covering the four forces of flight, basic performance calculations for range and endurance, stability and control concepts, and a short history of aircraft configuration development. Simple hand calculations for climb rate, takeoff distance, and glide ratio give students a working vocabulary before more rigorous aerodynamics and performance courses. No prior aerospace coursework is assumed.

Covers compressible flow fundamentals: the speed of sound, isentropic flow relations, normal and oblique shock waves, and flow through converging-diverging nozzles. Students work through Fanno and Rayleigh flow problems and learn to read compressible flow tables before any computational treatment is introduced. The course sets up the physical vocabulary that propulsion and high-speed aerodynamics courses build on later.

course_title: Experimental Methods in Aerospace Engineering II
course_desc: Building on basic instrumentation skills, this course moves into hot-wire anemometry, particle image velocimetry, and high-speed data acquisition for unsteady flow measurement. Students design their own test procedures rather than following a fixed protocol, then defend their methodology in a written report. Signal noise, sensor bandwidth, and calibration drift are treated as engineering problems in their own right, not just sources of error to be tolerated.

The second laboratory sequence moves to supersonic wind tunnel operation, vibration testing of cantilevered beams, and rotor balance measurements on a small-scale propeller rig. Students work in teams to design a test plan for one open-ended experiment chosen from a short list of options, then present findings alongside the standard written report. Instrumentation calibration and schlieren flow visualization are introduced for the first time here. Laboratory companion to AERO-2005.

Takes the systems perspective of the introductory course further into a full conceptual design exercise: weight estimation, mission sizing, configuration trade studies, and the iteration loop between subsystem requirements and vehicle performance. Teams carry a chosen aircraft or small spacecraft concept from a mission statement through a preliminary design review. Written and oral deliverables mirror the milestones used in industry design reviews.

Surveys the major propulsion types used in flight vehicles: turbojet, turbofan, turboprop, and rocket cycles, analyzed through thermodynamic cycle analysis and thrust and specific impulse calculations. Component-level treatment of inlets, compressors, combustors, and nozzles connects cycle performance to hardware constraints. Problem sets compare cycle choices across flight regimes, from subsonic transport to high-altitude cruise.

Applies structural mechanics to the thin-walled, weight-critical construction typical of aircraft and spacecraft: stress analysis of stiffened panels, shear flow in open and closed sections, buckling of columns and plates, and an introduction to composite laminate behavior. Design problems use realistic wing and fuselage cross-sections rather than idealized beams. Margin of safety calculations are carried through as the course's running deliverable.

Derives the equations of motion for a rigid aircraft and uses them to study longitudinal and lateral-directional stability, trim conditions, and the response to control surface deflection. Classical control techniques, including root locus and frequency response methods, are applied to design simple stability augmentation and autopilot loops. Simulation exercises let students see how stability derivatives shape handling qualities.

Extends numerical flow simulation from simple model equations into full Navier-Stokes solvers: finite volume discretization, upwind schemes, turbulence closure models, and mesh generation for realistic geometries. Students run and post-process simulations of flow over airfoils and simple three-dimensional bodies, comparing solver output against experimental or analytical benchmarks. Grid convergence studies and solution verification are treated as required practice, not optional extras.

A focused, advanced treatment of gas-turbine engines: compressor and turbine stage design, off-design performance mapping, combustor stability, and the mechanical and thermal constraints that limit real engine operation. Students work through component matching problems that connect thermodynamic cycle choices to achievable hardware performance. Case studies of production engine families illustrate how design trade-offs play out in practice.

Moves beyond continuum gas dynamics into the kinetic theory regime relevant to rarefied and high-altitude flows: the Boltzmann equation, mean free path effects, and the breakdown of continuum assumptions at low density or small length scale. Direct simulation Monte Carlo methods are introduced as the standard computational tool for this regime. Applications include reentry vehicle aerodynamics and low-Earth-orbit drag estimation.

Formal optimization methods are applied to problems that span multiple engineering disciplines at once: gradient-based and gradient-free algorithms, sensitivity analysis, surrogate modeling, and the coupling schemes needed when aerodynamic, structural, and propulsion models must be solved together. Students formulate and solve a multidisciplinary optimization problem of their own choosing as the term project. The course emphasizes problem formulation as much as algorithm mechanics.

Covers vibration and dynamic response of aerospace structures: modal analysis, forced response to harmonic and transient loading, and the onset of flutter in lifting surfaces. Finite element models built in earlier coursework are extended to include mass and damping matrices for dynamic simulation. Ground vibration testing and frequency response measurement give students a direct check against analytical predictions.

A senior-level synthesis of solid mechanics theory and aerospace structural application: three-dimensional stress and strain analysis, failure and fatigue criteria, and design of composite and metallic structures under combined loading. Students work through a structural sizing problem that carries from initial load case definition to a documented margin of safety. The course assumes fluency with thin-walled analysis from earlier structures coursework and pushes into fully three-dimensional treatment.

Covers the engineering and programmatic side of spacecraft development: orbital mechanics fundamentals, subsystem budgeting for power, thermal, and communications, and the systems engineering processes, including requirements management and review milestones, that govern real space programs. A term-long design project has students produce a mission concept document and a preliminary systems budget for a small satellite. Cost and schedule constraints are treated as design variables, not afterthoughts.

course_title: Special Topics in Flight Dynamics and Control
course_desc: Topics rotate by offering and cover current research and advanced practice in flight dynamics and control beyond the core sequence. Recent offerings have included nonlinear flight control, adaptive control for damaged aircraft, and control allocation for unconventional vehicle configurations. Readings are drawn from recent journal literature and paired with a substantial project or paper, and the specific topic changes each time the course is offered.

Topics rotate by offering and cover advanced compressible flow subjects not treated in the core gas dynamics sequence. Recent offerings have included hypersonic boundary layers, real-gas effects at high temperature, and detonation wave propagation. Students engage directly with current research papers and complete an independent analysis or computational project on the semester's chosen topic.

Introductory experiments cover fluid flow measurement, heat exchanger performance, and basic separation processes such as distillation on bench-scale apparatus. Each session pairs a safety and procedure briefing with data collection, and students submit formal lab reports comparing measured performance against theoretical models. The course establishes the reporting format, unit conversion discipline, and error propagation used throughout the laboratory sequence. Laboratory companion to CHEM-1010.

Introduces the core unit operations of chemical processing: fluid flow through pipes and pumps, heat exchanger design, and basic mass transfer in separation equipment such as distillation columns. Mass and energy balances anchor every problem set, connecting equipment sizing to the underlying conservation principles. The course builds the calculation habits that later, more specialized unit operations coursework assumes are already automatic.

Covers the laws of thermodynamics as applied to chemical process systems: energy and entropy balances, equations of state, and phase equilibrium calculations for pure components and simple mixtures. Problem sets move from closed system energy balances to vapor-liquid equilibrium diagrams used in separation design. The course establishes the thermodynamic vocabulary that unit operations and reactor design courses depend on later.

Applies probability and statistics to engineering data: descriptive statistics, hypothesis testing, regression, and design of experiments, worked through examples drawn from process and quality data rather than abstract problem sets. Students use statistical software to analyze a real or simulated dataset as a term project. The course also introduces structured problem-solving approaches used in engineering practice, including root-cause analysis.

Introduces the unified treatment of momentum, heat, and mass transfer that underlies chemical engineering analysis: shell balances, Fick's and Fourier's laws, and the analogies between the three transport modes. Students derive governing differential equations for simple geometries such as flow between plates or through a pipe before solving them. The course lays the mathematical groundwork for later unit operations and reactor design coursework.

Covers the engineering of biologically produced drugs: bioreactor design and scale-up, cell culture kinetics, downstream purification steps such as chromatography, and the regulatory constraints particular to biologic manufacturing. Case studies of monoclonal antibody and vaccine production illustrate how process decisions are shaped by product purity and consistency requirements. Problem sets connect fermentation kinetics to reactor sizing and yield calculations.

Covers the economic analysis tools used to evaluate chemical processes: capital and operating cost estimation, time value of money, net present value and rate of return calculations, and sensitivity analysis under price and demand uncertainty. Students build a cost estimate and economic evaluation for a process flowsheet developed in earlier coursework. The course treats economic feasibility as a design constraint on equal footing with technical performance.

Extends unit operations into more demanding separation and reaction equipment: multicomponent distillation, absorption and stripping columns, and an introduction to reactor sizing for continuous stirred-tank and plug-flow configurations. Design problems require students to size equipment against a specified production target rather than simply verify given performance. Process simulation software is introduced to check hand calculations against a rigorous model.

Builds on introductory laboratory skills with more complex unit operations: a packed-bed reactor, a multistage distillation column, and a membrane separation rig. Students work in teams to plan an experimental campaign for one open-ended process problem, then present results alongside a written report benchmarked against a process simulation. Process control loop tuning is introduced for the first time in this sequence. Laboratory companion to CHEM-2015.

Focuses on formulated and structured products rather than bulk commodity chemicals: consumer products, specialty coatings, and materials where microstructure and formulation drive performance as much as composition. Students work through a product design project from customer need identification to a formulated prototype and a supporting technical justification. Sensory and performance testing methods used in industry are introduced alongside traditional process calculations.

A rigorous treatment of fluid mechanics fundamentals: the Navier-Stokes equations, dimensional analysis and similarity, laminar and turbulent internal flow, and boundary layer behavior over submerged bodies. Applications are drawn from both process piping systems and open-channel and external flow problems, reflecting the course's shared audience. Problem sets require students to select and justify appropriate simplifying assumptions rather than apply a single fixed method. Cross-listed with CIVL-1040.

Examines the quality management systems that govern chemical and pharmaceutical manufacturing on a global scale: good manufacturing practice, statistical process control, root-cause investigation, and the documentation trail regulators expect. Case studies of manufacturing deviations and recalls illustrate how quality failures propagate through a supply chain. Students draft a quality system document for a hypothetical process as the course's main deliverable.

Covers the physical behavior of polymeric materials: chain conformation and molecular weight distribution, glass transition and crystallization, viscoelasticity, and the rheological measurements used to characterize melt and solution behavior. Problem sets connect molecular structure to bulk mechanical and thermal properties observed in processing. The course serves both chemical engineering and materials students, reflected in its dual listing. Cross-listed with MATL-2005.

Supervised independent work on a chemical engineering problem chosen in consultation with a faculty advisor, ranging from a literature-based analysis to original experimental or computational research. Students submit a short research proposal at the outset and a written technical report at the end of the term. The scope is calibrated to a single semester's effort and does not assume prior research experience.

A continuation track for students with prior independent research experience in the department, carrying a project into greater depth or over more than one semester. Students are expected to propose their own research question, defend their methodology to their advisor, and produce a report suitable as a foundation for a conference presentation or further study. Regular progress checkpoints replace the single end-of-term milestone used in the introductory research course.

Surveys current approaches to engineering biological tissue: scaffold materials and fabrication methods, cell seeding and bioreactor culture, and the transport limitations that govern nutrient and oxygen delivery within engineered constructs. Recent literature on organ-on-chip systems and 3D bioprinting supplements the core coverage. Students critique a current research paper and propose an extension as a term assignment.

A capstone-level treatment of process flowsheet development using commercial simulation tools: thermodynamic model selection, unit operation blocks, recycle convergence, and heat integration across a complete process. Teams carry a process from a preliminary flowsheet through a simulated, heat-integrated design with supporting economic evaluation. The course requires fluency with the unit operations and thermodynamics coverage from earlier semesters.

Applies reaction engineering principles to the design of complete reaction systems within a larger process context: reactor selection among competing configurations, catalyst deactivation, and the trade-offs between conversion, selectivity, and downstream separation cost. Students complete a design project that selects and sizes a reactor system against a stated production and purity target. Economic and safety constraints are folded into the design decision alongside kinetics.

Covers the fundamentals of chemical reactor analysis: rate law determination from kinetic data, design equations for batch, continuous stirred-tank, and plug-flow reactors, and the effects of temperature and mixing on conversion. Non-ideal flow patterns and residence time distribution are introduced to explain deviations from ideal reactor performance. Problem sets emphasize deriving and solving design equations rather than selecting between finished reactor configurations.

Topics rotate by offering and cover emerging areas of chemical engineering practice not addressed elsewhere in the curriculum. Recent offerings have included electrochemical process engineering, carbon capture technology, and machine learning applications in process monitoring. Students engage with current literature and complete a project or paper on the semester's chosen topic, and the subject matter changes each time the course is offered.

course_title: Special Topics in Chemical Engineering I
course_desc: The first of a two-part special topics sequence, with content rotating by offering to cover advanced or emerging subject matter beyond the standard curriculum. Recent offerings have included nanomaterials synthesis, food process engineering, and battery manufacturing processes. Students read current research literature and complete an independent project tied to that semester's topic, and enrollment does not require having taken the second course.

course_title: Special Topics in Chemical Engineering II
course_desc: The second of a two-part special topics sequence, rotating in subject matter independently of the first course and open to students regardless of which they have taken. Recent offerings have included industrial biotechnology, process safety analytics, and sustainable polymer design. Coursework centers on current literature review and a substantial independent project rather than problem sets.

Ambient and indoor air pollution problems anchor this introduction to air quality engineering, covering criteria pollutants, emission sources, and the atmospheric processes that govern dispersion. Students work through mass emission calculations, basic Gaussian plume estimates, and an overview of regulatory standards and monitoring networks. Control technologies for particulates and gaseous pollutants are surveyed at a conceptual level, setting up later coursework in process design.

Acid base equilibria, carbonate chemistry, and redox reactions in natural and engineered water systems form the core of this course. Coverage includes solubility and precipitation, complexation, and the chemical speciation calculations used to predict how contaminants behave in lakes, rivers, and treatment systems. Problem sets emphasize equilibrium modeling and interpreting water chemistry data rather than laboratory technique.

Bench experiments give hands-on grounding in the equilibrium concepts covered in the companion lecture, including titrations for alkalinity and hardness, pH and conductivity measurement, and simple precipitation and complexation trials. Students calibrate instruments, collect and reduce data, and write formal laboratory reports comparing measured results to equilibrium predictions. Laboratory companion to CIVL-1010.

Microbial growth kinetics, metabolism, and the biochemistry of aerobic and anaerobic treatment systems introduce students to the living side of environmental engineering. Topics include substrate utilization models, nitrification and denitrification, and the microbial ecology of activated sludge and biofilm reactors. The course builds the biological foundation later applied to treatment process design.

Parametric 3D modeling software and the BIM workflow are introduced through building and infrastructure case studies, covering model authoring, clash detection, and quantity takeoff. Students build discipline specific models and coordinate them across architectural, structural, and mechanical layers to catch conflicts before construction. Coursework also covers model based scheduling and the data standards that let BIM models move between project teams.

Standard tests on concrete, steel, asphalt, and wood specimens let students observe firsthand the mechanical behavior covered in the companion lecture, including tension and compression testing, slump and air content measurement, and failure mode analysis. Each session produces raw data that students reduce into stress strain curves and material property reports. Laboratory companion to CIVL-1035.

Concrete, steel, wood, and asphalt are examined through their microstructure, mechanical properties, and modes of failure, giving students a materials science grounding for later design courses. Topics include stress strain behavior, durability and deterioration mechanisms, and the standard specifications used to select materials for structural and pavement applications. Lectures connect material behavior to real construction failures and case histories.

A rigorous treatment of fluid mechanics fundamentals: the Navier-Stokes equations, dimensional analysis and similarity, laminar and turbulent internal flow, and boundary layer behavior over submerged bodies. Applications are drawn from both process piping systems and open-channel and external flow problems, reflecting the course's shared audience. Problem sets require students to select and justify appropriate simplifying assumptions rather than apply a single fixed method. Cross-listed with CHEM-3005.

Flow measurement and hydraulic apparatus form the core of this laboratory, with experiments on pipe friction losses, open channel flow over weirs, pump performance curves, and flow visualization in a recirculating flume. Students collect pressure and flow rate data, compute friction factors and discharge coefficients, and write reports comparing measured results to theoretical predictions. Laboratory companion to CIVL-1040.

Material and energy flows through industrial and urban systems are analyzed using life cycle assessment, material flow analysis, and industrial symbiosis case studies. Students quantify the environmental footprint of products and processes, compare design alternatives on embodied energy and waste generation, and examine how by products from one process can become inputs to another. The course frames sustainability as a systems accounting problem rather than a single technology fix.

Sensor technologies used to monitor bridges, pavements, pipelines, and buildings are surveyed, from strain gauges and accelerometers to fiber optics and remote imaging. Students learn how sensor networks are placed, sampled, and calibrated, and how the resulting data streams feed condition assessment and structural health monitoring. Case studies cover instrumented infrastructure and the tradeoffs between sensor cost, coverage, and data quality.

Core sustainability concepts for engineering practice are introduced, including life cycle thinking, resource efficiency, and a triple bottom line framework for weighing environmental, economic, and social outcomes. Students apply simple screening tools to compare design alternatives for energy use, materials, and waste, drawing examples from buildings, transportation, and water systems. The course serves as a conceptual foundation rather than a design methods course.

Programming exercises implement the numerical methods covered in the companion lecture, including root finding, matrix solvers, and finite difference schemes applied to small civil engineering problems. Students write, debug, and validate their own code against hand calculations and provided benchmark solutions, then document results in short technical reports. Laboratory companion to CIVL-2010.

Numerical techniques for solving the algebraic and differential equations that arise in civil engineering analysis are developed, including root finding, linear systems, numerical integration, and finite difference approximations. Students study the accuracy, stability, and convergence tradeoffs of each method and apply them to structural, hydraulic, and geotechnical example problems. Emphasis stays on the mathematics and algorithms rather than any single software package.

Pipe networks, pump stations, and open channel conveyances are sized in this design oriented course covering pressurized flow, pump selection curves, and uniform and gradually varied open channel flow. Students design water distribution and stormwater conveyance systems, checking head losses, surge effects, and channel capacity against design storms. Coursework culminates in a system design project with hydraulic calculations and drawings.

Bench and pilot scale experiments cover water and wastewater treatment unit processes, including coagulation flocculation jar tests, filtration, disinfection kinetics, and biochemical oxygen demand measurement. Students collect samples, run standard analytical methods for common water quality parameters, and interpret results against treatment performance targets. Reports emphasize connecting measured removal efficiencies to the underlying treatment mechanism. Laboratory companion to CIVL-2025.

Mass balances on pollutants moving through natural and engineered systems anchor this course, applied to lakes, groundwater, and treatment trains alike. Students quantify how contaminants partition, degrade, and accumulate using reaction kinetics and mass balance models, and interpret water and air quality parameters such as dissolved oxygen, biochemical oxygen demand, and particulate concentration against regulatory standards. Later sessions size treatment processes as chemistry and mass balance problems, sequencing unit operations to meet an effluent or ambient target.

Soil classification, effective stress, consolidation, and shear strength are introduced as the basis for analyzing how soils support and interact with civil infrastructure. Students work through settlement calculations, bearing capacity estimates, and slope stability screening using classical soil mechanics methods. Site investigation techniques and the interpretation of boring logs and laboratory soil tests round out the course.

Standard geotechnical tests give hands-on experience with the soil behavior covered in the companion lecture, including sieve and hydrometer gradation, Atterberg limits, compaction, and direct shear testing. Students prepare specimens, run each test to specification, and reduce raw readings into classification and strength parameters used in design. Laboratory companion to CIVL-2030.

Structural behavior beyond first yield is the subject here, covering plastic hinge formation, moment redistribution, and limit state collapse mechanisms in steel frames and continuous beams. Students apply upper and lower bound theorems to find collapse loads and compare plastic design capacity against conventional elastic design assumptions. The course extends earlier structural analysis coursework into inelastic behavior and ultimate strength.

Breadboard exercises build the electronics foundation behind the companion lecture, including wiring analog and digital sensor circuits, signal conditioning with op amps and filters, and basic microcontroller data logging. Students calibrate sensors against known references, troubleshoot noisy circuits, and document each build in a lab notebook and short report. Laboratory companion to CIVL-2050.

Electrical fundamentals needed to instrument civil and environmental systems are covered, including circuit analysis, sensor transduction principles, signal conditioning, and analog to digital conversion. Students study strain, pressure, temperature, and displacement sensors and how their output is filtered, amplified, and logged for engineering monitoring applications. The course assumes no prior electronics background and builds toward instrumentation design.

Contract types, bidding procedures, and risk allocation between owners, designers, and contractors are examined through the legal and business structure of construction projects. Students review delivery methods such as design bid build and design build, analyze sample contract clauses, and work through change order and claims scenarios. The course builds the business literacy needed to manage a construction project rather than design one.

Simulated project scenarios let students practice the contracting skills covered in the companion lecture, including preparing a competitive bid package, negotiating a mock change order, and drafting a claims response memo. Teams role play owner, contractor, and designer positions and present their positions in a short mock negotiation. Laboratory companion to CIVL-3005.

course_title: Data Analysis in Civil and Environmental Engineering
course_desc: Statistical methods for analyzing field and laboratory data are developed for civil and environmental applications, covering regression, hypothesis testing, and uncertainty propagation. Students work with real infrastructure and monitoring datasets to fit trend lines, screen for outliers, and quantify confidence in design parameters derived from limited samples. The course emphasizes defensible data interpretation over software mechanics.

course_title: Design of Reinforced Concrete Structures Laboratory
course_desc: Physical models and instrumented specimens illustrate the reinforced concrete behavior covered in the companion lecture, including beam and slab load tests to observe cracking, deflection, and failure mode. Students instrument test specimens with strain gauges, record load deflection response, and compare measured capacity to hand calculated design values. Laboratory companion to CIVL-3025.

Flexural, shear, and axial design of reinforced concrete beams, slabs, and columns is developed from first principles of strain compatibility and equilibrium. Students size reinforcement for strength and serviceability limit states, check deflection and crack control requirements, and complete a multi member design project following standard design provisions. The course assumes prior coursework in structural analysis and mechanics of materials.

Unit operations used in water and wastewater treatment trains are designed at the reactor level, covering sedimentation basin sizing, filter design, activated sludge reactor kinetics, and disinfection contact time. Students size individual treatment processes against loading and effluent targets, then sequence them into a complete treatment train, incorporating hydraulic profile and flow rate considerations across the plant. The course builds directly on introductory environmental engineering coursework into process scale design.

Methods for excavating and supporting underground and below grade construction are covered, including open cut excavation bracing, shoring and dewatering systems, and tunnel boring and ground support techniques. Students evaluate ground conditions and construction sequencing to select appropriate excavation methods and estimate support loads. Case studies cover urban excavation challenges and tunneling projects through varied ground conditions.

Pretensioned and post tensioned concrete member design is developed, covering prestress losses, transfer and development length, and flexural and shear capacity of prestressed sections. Students design bridge girders and building members for both service load and ultimate strength limit states, accounting for camber and long term losses. The course extends reinforced concrete design principles into prestressing applications.

Engineering ethics, licensure, liability, and professional practice standards are examined alongside a capstone style design exercise that integrates prior coursework into a single project. Students research codes and standards applicable to their project, document design decisions, and present their work to a review panel. Case studies of engineering failures and ethical lapses anchor discussion of professional responsibility.

Probabilistic methods for quantifying structural safety are introduced, covering random variable modeling of loads and resistance, reliability indices, and the calibration of load and resistance factors used in design codes. Students compute failure probabilities for simple structural elements and compare deterministic safety factors to reliability based design approaches. The course connects probability theory directly to the safety margins embedded in structural design codes.

Equilibrium of rigid bodies, internal force analysis, and the kinematics and kinetics of particles and rigid bodies are developed as the mechanics foundation for structural and geotechnical design. Students analyze truss and frame systems for internal forces and work through vector mechanics problems involving motion, momentum, and vibration. Problem sets move from static free body analysis to dynamic response under time varying loads.

Building on introductory soil mechanics, this course develops critical state soil mechanics, advanced consolidation theory, and constitutive models for predicting nonlinear soil stress strain behavior. Students work through laboratory data interpretation for triaxial and consolidation tests and apply advanced settlement and deformation analyses to layered and anisotropic soil profiles. The course prepares students to evaluate soil behavior beyond the simplified models used in introductory design.

Current research literature in construction engineering is surveyed, covering topics such as productivity modeling, automation and robotics on the job site, and lean construction methods. Students critique published studies, identify open research questions, and complete a literature review paper on a construction engineering topic of their choosing. The course develops the critical reading and research synthesis skills used in graduate level construction engineering work.

Heavy construction equipment selection and the engineering behind earthmoving, lifting, and material handling operations are covered, including production rate estimating and equipment cost analysis. Students size equipment fleets for excavation and paving operations and evaluate productivity tradeoffs between machine types and crew configurations. Case studies cover large scale earthwork and heavy civil projects.

Civil infrastructure that generates, stores, and distributes energy is examined, including power plant siting, transmission corridor design, and the civil works associated with renewable generation such as wind and solar installations. Students evaluate site selection, permitting, and resilience considerations for energy infrastructure projects, and compare the civil engineering demands of conventional and renewable generation. The course treats energy systems as a civil infrastructure design problem rather than an electrical one.

Under faculty supervision, students propose and carry out an original research project in hydraulic or hydrologic engineering, chosen in consultation with a faculty advisor. Deliverables include a written proposal, a literature review, data collection or modeling work, and a final written report presented to the supervising faculty member. The format allows students to pursue a topic such as watershed modeling, channel design, or stormwater system performance in depth.

Earth retention and impoundment structures are analyzed, covering slope stability methods, retaining wall design, and the geotechnical design of earthen and concrete dams. Students evaluate failure surfaces and factors of safety for natural and engineered slopes, and size retaining structures and dam sections against overturning, sliding, and seepage related failure modes. Case studies examine historical slope and dam failures to illustrate design lessons.

Stress and strain tensors, constitutive relations, and energy methods are developed for analyzing deformable bodies beyond the rigid body assumptions of introductory mechanics. Students derive and apply theories of elasticity, torsion, and beam bending to problems in structural and mechanical component design, and use energy methods such as virtual work to solve indeterminate systems. The course provides the continuum mechanics foundation for advanced structural analysis.

course_title: Special Topics in Civil and Environmental Engineering
course_desc: Topics in this course rotate by offering and draw on current developments in civil and environmental engineering, with recent offerings covering resilient infrastructure design, climate adaptation engineering, and smart city sensing networks. Each offering is organized around readings, guest case studies, and a term project tailored to the semester's theme. Students should consult the current offering's topic description before enrolling.

Urban systems are examined through a sustainability lens, covering compact development, urban water and energy systems, green infrastructure, and transportation electrification at the city scale. Students analyze case studies of cities pursuing carbon reduction and climate resilience goals, and complete a project proposing sustainability interventions for a specific urban system. The course applies sustainability concepts at the scale of whole cities rather than individual buildings or products.

Algorithm design and analysis form the spine of this introductory course, covering asymptotic notation, divide-and-conquer, greedy strategies, and dynamic programming through problems like sorting, shortest paths, and interval scheduling. Students prove correctness and derive running-time bounds by hand before implementing solutions in code. Graph traversal (breadth-first and depth-first search) and an introduction to NP-completeness close out the term.

Hands-on exercises translate the architecture lecture into working hardware: students wire and simulate combinational and sequential logic circuits, build a simple datapath from adders, multiplexers, and registers, and step a toy instruction set through fetch-decode-execute by hand. Weekly lab reports document circuit diagrams, timing measurements, and debugging notes. Laboratory companion to COMP-1015.

Digital logic design anchors this introduction to how computers are built, moving from gates and flip-flops through combinational and sequential circuits to a complete single-cycle datapath and control unit. Coverage includes instruction set design, number representation, and an early look at pipelining as a performance technique. Problem sets emphasize tracing signals through a circuit rather than writing software.

A first look at how machines interpret images, covering image formation, pixel-level filtering, edge and corner detection, and simple color and shape based object recognition. Assignments use small, well-lit datasets to build intuition for why vision is hard before any heavy mathematics enters the picture. The course favors working demonstrations over derivation, previewing the geometric and statistical machinery taken up rigorously in advanced coursework.

Arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, and hash tables are introduced alongside the algorithms that operate on them, including basic sorting, searching, and traversal routines. Asymptotic analysis is taught as a practical tool for choosing between structures rather than as a standalone topic. Programming exercises require implementing each structure from scratch before using built-in equivalents.

Weekly exercises have students implement and benchmark the structures introduced in lecture, building a linked list, a binary search tree, and a hash table with collision handling, then timing each against a reference implementation. Later sessions add a small sorting-algorithm shootout and a short written report comparing measured performance to predicted asymptotic behavior. Laboratory companion to COMP-1025.

Propositional and predicate logic, proof techniques such as induction and contradiction, set theory, and an introduction to finite automata give incoming students the discrete-mathematics toolkit the rest of the curriculum assumes. Short weekly proofs build fluency before larger constructions like regular expressions and simple state machines. The course treats computation as a mathematical object rather than as programming practice.

Students probe deliberately vulnerable sample applications to find and exploit common weaknesses such as buffer overflows, SQL injection, and weak password storage, then patch the same code and verify the fix. Later exercises cover setting up a basic firewall and encrypting files with a symmetric cipher. Each session ends with a short writeup of what was broken and how it was fixed. Laboratory companion to COMP-1045.

An entry-level survey of why systems get compromised, covering common attack categories, basic cryptographic primitives, authentication, and secure coding habits like input validation. Case studies of real breaches illustrate how small design mistakes lead to large consequences. The course assumes no prior security background and builds vocabulary and threat models used throughout later coursework.

This course takes the programmer's view of the machine: number representation, memory hierarchy, assembly-language programming, and how high-level code is translated into instructions the processor executes. Labs trace variable values through registers and memory as a program runs. The emphasis stays on what a working programmer needs to know about the underlying hardware rather than on circuit-level design.

A first pass through supervised and unsupervised learning, covering linear and logistic regression, k-nearest neighbors, decision trees, and k-means clustering, with an emphasis on applying existing libraries correctly rather than deriving methods from scratch. Students work through a sequence of small labeled datasets to build intuition for overfitting and model evaluation. The course is designed as an on-ramp for students who have not taken a statistics-heavy math sequence.

Processes, threads, scheduling algorithms, virtual memory, and file systems are examined both conceptually and through kernel-level code walkthroughs. Programming assignments implement a simple scheduler and a basic memory allocator on a teaching operating system. The course frames each mechanism as a solution to a specific resource-sharing problem rather than as an isolated feature to memorize.

Game design is treated as an engineering discipline here, covering the rendering pipeline, collision detection, game loops and frame timing, and basic AI for non-player characters, alongside design fundamentals like pacing, difficulty curves, and player feedback loops. Teams prototype and playtest a small original game over the term, iterating on mechanics based on observed player behavior. Readings draw on both established game engines and design case studies.

Exercises move from packet capture and traffic analysis to configuring firewall rules, setting up an intrusion detection sensor, and staging a controlled man-in-the-middle attack against unencrypted traffic to see why transport-layer encryption matters. Each lab produces a short incident report describing what was observed and how the network was hardened afterward. Laboratory companion to COMP-2025.

Network-layer and transport-layer attacks, including spoofing, denial of service, and traffic interception, are examined alongside the defenses built to counter them: firewalls, intrusion detection systems, and protocols like TLS and VPN tunneling. Case studies trace how real incidents exploited gaps between protocol design and deployment. The course assumes familiarity with basic networking concepts and builds toward designing a defensible network topology.

Students build a working compiler in stages across the term, starting with a lexical analyzer and recursive-descent parser, moving through semantic analysis and type checking, and finishing with code generation for a simplified target machine. Each stage is graded against a shared test suite so bugs surface early rather than at the end. The course treats the compiler pipeline as a template for any tool that translates one structured language into another.

The relational model, normalization, and query design form the core of this course, taught through extensive practice writing and optimizing structured queries against realistic schemas. Later weeks cover transaction management, concurrency control, and indexing strategies that keep large databases fast and consistent. A term project has students design a schema from a set of business requirements and defend their normalization choices.

Building on a probability and linear algebra foundation, this course develops the mathematics behind regression, classification, and clustering methods, including gradient-based optimization, regularization, and bias-variance tradeoffs. Students implement core algorithms rather than only calling library functions, and a project applies cross-validation to select among competing models on a nontrivial dataset. A brief unit introduces feedforward neural networks as a bridge to further study.

This advanced course treats data structures as engineering decisions made under real constraints: cache behavior, memory footprint, and concurrent access all shape which structure belongs in a given system. Topics include balanced trees, tries, disjoint-set structures, and lock-free queues, each implemented and profiled rather than taken on faith. A substantial project embeds several of these structures inside a larger piece of software and measures the effect of each choice on overall performance.

Lab sessions have students implement, profile, and tune the structures covered in lecture inside a shared codebase, measuring cache misses and allocation overhead rather than only asymptotic complexity. A multi-week capstone exercise integrates several structures into one small system and requires a written performance analysis. Laboratory companion to COMP-3005.

Perception, memory, and reasoning are examined through computational models drawn from both symbolic AI and connectionist networks, with readings pairing each model against experimental data from cognitive psychology. Students implement small simulations, such as an associative memory network or a rule-based reasoning system, and compare their output to published human performance data. The course sits at the boundary between cognitive science and artificial intelligence.

This advanced treatment develops the mathematics underlying modern vision systems: projective geometry, camera calibration, epipolar geometry for stereo reconstruction, and optimization methods used to fit models to noisy image data. Derivations are carried through in detail and then verified against implemented code on real image sequences. The course assumes comfort with linear algebra and prepares students to read current vision research rather than only apply existing tools.

Multicore processor design, cache coherence protocols, and vector and SIMD execution units are covered alongside the programming models used to exploit them, including shared-memory threading and data-parallel kernels. Case studies compare architectural tradeoffs across real multicore and accelerator designs. Lab-style exercises measure speedup and identify contention as parallelism increases on actual hardware.

Requirements gathering, architectural design, version control discipline, automated testing, and code review are practiced across a semester-long team project rather than taught as separate topics. Design patterns and common architectural styles are introduced as vocabulary for discussing tradeoffs, not as rules to follow blindly. Teams present their system's evolution, including decisions later reversed, as part of the final deliverable.

Classical search, knowledge representation, first-order logic, and automated planning form the theoretical core of this senior-level course, with each topic grounded in worked examples such as puzzle-solving agents and constraint satisfaction problems. A short unit on learning agents previews the statistical methods taken up in dedicated machine learning courses. Problem sets emphasize formal representation and proof over implementation.

Building directly on classical AI foundations, this course covers modern deep learning architectures, reinforcement learning, and multi-agent systems, with readings drawn from current research papers rather than a fixed textbook. Students reproduce results from a recent paper and extend or critique the approach in a final project. Discussion sections function as a seminar, evaluating claims and comparing competing architectures.

Human-computer interaction principles, including cognitive load, affordance, and accessibility, are paired with hands-on prototyping and usability testing across the term. Students build interactive prototypes, run structured usability sessions with real test subjects, and revise designs based on observed friction points rather than intuition alone. The course closes with a comparative evaluation of two interface designs for the same task.

Students stand up a multi-tier web application from scratch, wiring a client, an application server, and a persistent data store together, then load-test the result and diagnose the resulting bottlenecks. Later sessions add authentication, input sanitization, and a deployment behind a reverse proxy. Each milestone requires a short report on what broke under load and how it was fixed. Laboratory companion to COMP-4025.

Client-server architecture, statelessness, caching layers, and the protocols that hold a modern web application together are examined at senior depth, including how systems are designed to scale under load and resist common attacks like injection and cross-site scripting. Case studies trace real outages back to violated assumptions about request volume or trust boundaries. The course assumes prior programming experience and treats the web as a distributed system, not a single application.

A survey of the political, economic, and social forces that shaped the nation from its founding through the twentieth century, read through primary documents alongside standard narrative accounts. Discussion sections weigh competing interpretations of major turning points rather than settling on a single account. Required of all students as part of the general-education core, it gives engineers grounding in the civic and institutional context their later careers operate within.

Limits, derivatives, and integrals are developed from first principles and applied to rates of change, optimization, and area and volume problems, building the mathematical language used throughout the engineering curriculum. Multivariable extensions late in the term set up the vector calculus that later coursework in circuits, mechanics, and signal processing assumes. Weekly problem sets emphasize technique alongside the reasoning behind each rule.

Close reading of poetry, drama, and prose from several periods sharpens the written and analytical communication skills every engineer eventually needs to explain a design decision or a failure. Students write a series of short critical essays rather than a single term paper, building the habit of a tight, well-supported argument. Discussion sections favor textual evidence over general impression.

The mechanics of the balance sheet, income statement, and cash flow statement are taught through practice building and reading financial statements for real and simulated companies. Coverage includes accrual accounting, depreciation methods, and the limits of accounting numbers as a picture of a company's health. Engineers who later manage budgets or evaluate vendors use the vocabulary and structure taught here.

Time value of money, discounted cash flow analysis, capital budgeting, and the basics of how firms are valued and financed round out the core's coverage of how organizations make and justify spending decisions. Problem sets require evaluating competing investment options under stated assumptions about risk and return. The course gives engineers the financial literacy to build a business case for a proposed project.

Organizational structure, team leadership, and the practical mechanics of planning and running a project are covered through case discussions and a short simulation exercise. Students examine how the same engineering decision plays out differently under different management structures and incentive systems. The course prepares students to lead teams and manage tradeoffs, not just execute assigned tasks.

Contracts, intellectual property, liability, and the basics of how businesses are legally structured are covered through case studies drawn from real disputes. Particular attention goes to how these issues arise in technology and engineering contexts, including patent disputes and product liability. Students learn to recognize when a decision carries legal exposure worth flagging to counsel, not to act as their own lawyer.

Random variables, common probability distributions, hypothesis testing, and regression are developed with an eye toward the experimental design and data analysis engineers perform throughout their careers. Problem sets use datasets drawn from engineering contexts, such as measurement error and reliability testing, rather than abstract examples. The course provides the statistical foundation assumed by later coursework in machine learning and experimental methods.

Disordered semiconductors such as amorphous silicon and chalcogenide glasses depart from the periodic lattice assumptions of standard device theory, and this course builds the physical picture needed to understand them: band tails, localized states, and variable-range hopping transport. Students compare density-of-states models against transport measurements and connect the physics to thin-film transistors, photovoltaic cells, and memory switching devices. Problem sets emphasize order-of-magnitude estimation over closed-form solutions, since amorphous materials rarely offer one.

Operational amplifiers, diodes, and bipolar and field-effect transistors form the building blocks covered here, starting from DC biasing and small-signal models and moving through amplifier stages, active filters, and basic oscillators. Circuit analysis is paired with practical design tradeoffs such as gain-bandwidth limits, input offset, and output loading. The course establishes the vocabulary and hand-analysis techniques that later integrated-circuit and RF courses assume.

Bench work here has students build and troubleshoot the amplifier, filter, and biasing circuits introduced in lecture, using oscilloscopes, function generators, and multimeters to characterize gain, bandwidth, and distortion. Each session ends with a short written report comparing measured performance against hand-calculated predictions and explaining any discrepancies. Laboratory companion to EENG-1010.

Where introductory circuit courses treat transistors as discrete parts on a breadboard, this course studies them as they behave inside an integrated circuit: current mirrors, differential pairs, and cascode stages built from matched devices sharing a common substrate. Coverage includes bias and reference generation, multistage operational amplifier topologies, and the layout and matching considerations that separate integrated design from board-level design. Students work through hand calculations of gain, bandwidth, and noise for representative amplifier architectures.

Radiation from current distributions is derived from first principles here, starting with the elementary dipole and building through gain, directivity, and polarization to array factor calculations for linear arrays. Design exercises ask students to size a dipole or patch element for a target frequency and input impedance, then verify the result against a simulated radiation pattern. The course treats antennas as a design problem in electromagnetics rather than a component chosen from a catalog.

Feedback systems are modeled with transfer functions and block diagrams, then analyzed for stability and transient response using root locus and frequency-response methods. The course covers proportional-integral-derivative compensation and lead-lag design, applying each technique to examples like a motor speed regulator or a temperature control loop. Simulation exercises let students verify hand designs against a simulated plant before committing to a controller.

Kirchhoff's current and voltage laws, resistive networks, and first-order RC and RL transients are introduced alongside a survey of where they show up in practice, from power distribution to sensor interfaces to simple communication links. The course balances hand analysis of small networks with brief case studies that connect circuit behavior to the systems built from it. It is designed as a broad entry point into circuit thinking for students who will specialize later rather than a deep dive into any single application.

course_title: Electric Circuits, Systems, and Applications Laboratory
course_desc: Breadboard exercises here walk through building the resistive networks and RC and RL transient circuits covered in lecture, measuring voltage and current with a digital multimeter and oscilloscope and comparing the results to predicted time constants. Later sessions assemble small application circuits, such as a sensor interface or a power-supply filter, and ask students to diagnose wiring and measurement errors when results do not match theory. Laboratory companion to EENG-1035.

Variables, conditionals, loops, and functions form the core vocabulary taught here, building toward simple data structures such as arrays and records and basic file input and output. Weekly exercises move from short scripts that manipulate numbers and text to small programs that process a data set and report summary statistics. The course assumes no prior programming background and emphasizes reading error messages and testing code incrementally over memorizing syntax.

Guided lab sessions have students write, run, and debug the short programs introduced in lecture, working through arrays, loops, and simple file handling with an instructor checking logic before code is submitted. Later weeks assign small standalone programs, such as a grade-averaging tool or a basic unit converter, that must pass a set of test inputs. Laboratory companion to EENG-1045.

Microfabrication is presented as a sequence of process steps: photolithography, thin-film deposition, wet and dry etching, and packaging. Students design a simple microsystem layout, such as a cantilever sensor or a microfluidic channel, that could in principle be carried through those steps, working with design rules, mask layout, and process tolerances alongside the physics of each fabrication technique. The emphasis throughout is on the manufacturing pipeline rather than on the electrical behavior of the finished device.

Students characterize packaged microsystem devices such as accelerometers and pressure sensors on the bench, measuring sensitivity, offset, and noise and building the signal-conditioning circuitry needed to read them out. Later sessions introduce a microfabricated test structure and ask students to relate its measured mechanical response to its design geometry. Laboratory companion to EENG-1055.

Microelectromechanical sensors and actuators are introduced here as complete systems: a pressure sensor, an accelerometer, or a micromirror is studied from its mechanical structure through the electronics that read or drive it. The course surveys common transduction mechanisms, capacitive, piezoresistive, and piezoelectric, and shows how each couples to signal-conditioning circuitry. Fabrication is discussed only at a conceptual level, leaving process detail to a companion design course.

Crystalline semiconductor physics is built up from energy bands and carrier statistics to the pn junction, then applied to explain diode current-voltage behavior and the basic operation of bipolar and field-effect transistors. Depletion regions, minority carrier injection, and threshold voltage are treated with enough mathematical detail to predict device behavior in each case. The course assumes ordered crystalline material throughout, leaving disordered and amorphous semiconductors to a separate course.

Discrete-time signals and systems are the subject here, covering sampling, the z-transform, difference equations, and the design of simple finite and infinite impulse response filters. Students move from continuous signals to their sampled representations and examine how aliasing, quantization, and filter order affect a processed waveform. Homework problems use short numerical exercises to connect the transform-domain theory to time-domain filtering results.

Microcontroller-based systems are introduced through their building blocks: general-purpose input and output pins, timers, interrupts, and serial communication peripherals. Students design simple event-driven programs that read a sensor, control an actuator, and communicate status over a serial link, learning to reason about timing constraints and limited memory along the way. The course treats hardware and firmware as a single design problem rather than teaching each in isolation.

course_title: Introduction to Embedded System Design Laboratory
course_desc: Weekly exercises have students wire a microcontroller development board to sensors and actuators and write firmware to drive them, progressing from a blinking indicator light to a small project such as a temperature-triggered fan controller. Oscilloscopes and logic analyzers are used to debug timing problems in interrupt handlers and serial communication. Laboratory companion to EENG-1080.

Combinational and sequential logic circuits built in lecture are implemented and tested here, first with discrete logic gates on a breadboard and later on a programmable logic device. Students verify truth tables and timing diagrams against oscilloscope and logic analyzer traces, and a final project asks them to design and debug a small finite-state machine such as a traffic-light controller. Laboratory companion to EENG-1095.

Boolean algebra, truth tables, and systematic minimization techniques provide the tools for reducing combinational logic to a small set of gates, and the course then extends to sequential circuits built from flip-flops, counters, and simple finite-state machines. Design examples range from an adder built from basic gates to a state machine controlling a small sequence of outputs. The course establishes the digital design foundation assumed by later courses in embedded systems and integrated circuits.

course_title: Introduction to Signals and Systems Laboratory
course_desc: Continuous and discrete signals generated in software and on the bench are analyzed here, with students measuring the impulse and frequency response of simple RC and RL circuits and comparing the results to convolution and Fourier predictions from lecture. A closing exercise has students design and test a basic filter against a target frequency response. Laboratory companion to EENG-2010.

Continuous-time and discrete-time signals are analyzed through convolution, Fourier series, and the Fourier and Laplace transforms, building a common mathematical language for the circuits, controls, and communications courses that follow. Linear time-invariant systems are characterized by impulse response and frequency response, with worked examples covering filtering, modulation, and sampling. The course treats these tools as a unified framework rather than a collection of unrelated transform tricks.

Radiation patterns of dipole, patch, and horn antennas are measured on an anechoic or open-range test setup, and students compare the measured gain, beamwidth, and polarization to simulated or specified values. A matching-network exercise has students tune an antenna's input impedance to a target frequency using a vector network analyzer. Laboratory companion to EENG-2020.

Antennas here are treated as system components rather than electromagnetics problems: the course surveys dipole, patch, horn, and reflector types by the tradeoffs an engineer actually chooses between, such as bandwidth, beamwidth, and ease of integration into a transmitter chain. Link budgets, standing wave ratio, and impedance matching networks connect antenna performance to overall system range and reliability. Case studies compare antenna choices across handset, base station, and satellite applications.

Node and mesh analysis techniques from lecture are verified on the bench here, with students building resistive networks and measuring node voltages and branch currents against hand calculations using Thevenin and Norton equivalents. Later sessions extend to AC steady-state measurements with a function generator and oscilloscope, checking phasor predictions against measured amplitude and phase. Laboratory companion to EENG-2030.

Node-voltage and mesh-current analysis, Thevenin and Norton equivalents, and superposition are developed for resistive networks and then extended to circuits with capacitors and inductors under sinusoidal steady-state excitation using phasors. Transient response of first- and second-order RLC circuits is solved using differential equations rather than the qualitative treatment given in earlier survey courses. The course is aimed at students who need a rigorous analytical toolkit before proceeding to devices and systems courses.

This course continues from the postulates of quantum mechanics into the Schrodinger equation for finite and infinite potential wells, tunneling, and the quantum harmonic oscillator, applying each result to explain electronic behavior in semiconductor structures. Perturbation theory and time-dependent problems are introduced to handle systems that lack closed-form solutions. Applications drawn from optoelectronics and nanoscale devices connect the mathematics to device behavior covered in parallel device courses.

Packet-switched network architecture is examined layer by layer, from framing and medium access control up through routing and basic transport protocols, using layered reference models to organize the material. Queueing delay, throughput, and error control are analyzed quantitatively for simple network topologies. Case studies cover wired local area networks and wireless access, contrasting their medium access and error-handling strategies.

Manufacturing defects in digital circuits are modeled as stuck-at and bridging faults, and the course develops automatic test pattern generation techniques to detect them, including path sensitization and fault simulation. Design-for-testability structures such as scan chains and built-in self-test are covered alongside the tradeoffs they impose on chip area and speed. Homework problems have students generate test vectors by hand for small combinational circuits before moving to tool-assisted methods.

DC, induction, and synchronous machines are analyzed through equivalent circuit models that predict torque, speed, and efficiency under varying load, and the course extends this to the power electronic drives that control them. Steady-state and basic dynamic behavior are covered for each machine type, along with the switching converter topologies commonly paired with them. Worked problems size a motor and drive combination for a target speed and torque profile.

Students run induction and DC machines on a test bench, measuring torque-speed curves with a dynamometer and comparing them to the equivalent circuit predictions developed in lecture. A later session connects a machine to a variable-frequency drive and records startup and speed-regulation behavior under changing load. Laboratory companion to EENG-2050.

Population inversion, optical gain, and cavity resonance are developed from rate equations to explain how a laser reaches threshold and produces coherent output, with gas, solid-state, and semiconductor gain media compared as worked examples. Cavity design, longitudinal mode structure, and output coupling are treated at an introductory level sufficient to estimate threshold current or pump power for a given design. The course builds the foundation that a later course extends into pulsed and high-power laser systems.

Two-level and multilevel logic minimization techniques are covered here, including tabular and algebraic factoring methods used to reduce gate count and propagation delay, along with the use of don't-care conditions to further simplify a design. Technology mapping onto standard cell libraries and programmable logic architectures is introduced alongside timing and area tradeoffs. Design exercises optimize a given logic function under competing area, delay, and power constraints.

Geometric and wave optics are covered together, moving from ray tracing through thin lenses and mirrors to interference, diffraction, and polarization phenomena explained by the wave nature of light. Diffraction gratings, thin-film interference, and simple imaging systems are analyzed quantitatively using worked examples. The course provides the optical foundation used by later courses in lasers and optoelectronic devices.

Random variables, probability distributions, and stochastic processes are developed with engineering applications in mind, covering topics such as noise in circuits, bit errors in communication links, and component reliability. Expectation, variance, and conditional probability are applied to worked problems drawn from signal detection and system reliability analysis. The course builds the probabilistic toolkit assumed by later courses in communications and detection theory.

Manufacturing lines are modeled as networks of workstations, buffers, and material flows, and the course covers throughput analysis, bottleneck identification, and scheduling techniques used to improve production system performance. Queueing and simulation models are applied to case studies such as a circuit-board assembly line or an electronics test station. Students build a simplified simulation of a production line and use it to evaluate proposed changes in staffing or buffer sizing. Cross-listed with MANU-3030.

Light-emitting diodes, laser diodes, and photodetectors are analyzed by connecting semiconductor band structure to optical absorption and emission, covering direct versus indirect bandgap materials, quantum efficiency, and responsivity. Solar cells are treated as a related device that converts absorbed photons into current rather than emitting light. Worked problems calculate emission wavelength, efficiency, or detector responsivity from given material parameters.

Students measure the current-voltage and light-output characteristics of light-emitting diodes and laser diodes, and use a photodetector setup to record responsivity as a function of wavelength. A closing experiment characterizes a small photovoltaic cell under varying illumination and computes its efficiency. Laboratory companion to EENG-3010.

Students design and simulate CMOS logic gates at the transistor level, laying out cells according to design rules and verifying that the layout matches the intended schematic before extracting parasitic capacitances for timing analysis. A final project has students assemble a small standard-cell block, such as a multiplexer or adder, and verify its function through simulation. Laboratory companion to EENG-3025.

CMOS transistor operation is applied to the design of static logic gates, covering pull-up and pull-down network construction, gate sizing for target delay, and the layout rules that govern how transistors are physically arranged on a chip. Propagation delay and power dissipation are estimated by hand using simplified transistor models before more detailed simulation is introduced. The course establishes the static design flow that a later course extends to dynamic circuits and memory.

Mobile robot navigation is built up from kinematic models of wheeled platforms through sensor fusion, localization, and path planning algorithms, connecting each topic to the perception and control problems a robot must solve to move through an environment. Coverage includes basic mapping techniques and obstacle avoidance strategies evaluated in simulation before any hardware is involved. Students implement a simplified planning algorithm and test it against a set of simulated environments.

Wheeled robot platforms are programmed here to execute the localization and path-planning algorithms introduced in lecture, using onboard sensors such as encoders and rangefinders to navigate a marked course. Teams iterate on a semester project that must complete a navigation task with a fixed budget of sensors and computation. Laboratory companion to EENG-3030.

Building on discrete-time system theory, this course focuses on designing filters to meet a target specification and implementing them under real hardware constraints such as fixed-point arithmetic, limited word length, and finite processor throughput. Filter design methods including windowing and equiripple approximation are compared for how closely they meet passband and stopband requirements. Students translate a filter specification into a working implementation and verify it against the target frequency response.

Filters designed in lecture are implemented on a signal-processing platform, with students measuring frequency response and quantifying the error introduced by fixed-point rounding relative to a floating-point reference. A closing project applies a designed filter to a recorded signal and evaluates whether it meets its passband and stopband targets. Laboratory companion to EENG-3040.

Signal-conditioning circuits for common sensors such as strain gauges, thermistors, and photodiodes are built and characterized here, with students measuring sensitivity and noise floor against datasheet specifications. A final exercise integrates a sensor, conditioning circuit, and simple readout display into a working measurement instrument. Laboratory companion to EENG-3055.

Transduction mechanisms for common sensors, resistive, capacitive, and photonic, are covered alongside the signal-conditioning circuitry needed to turn a small sensor output into a usable measurement: instrumentation amplifiers, bridge circuits, and filtering for noise rejection. Error sources such as drift, nonlinearity, and electromagnetic interference are analyzed with an eye toward practical measurement system design. Case studies cover strain measurement, temperature sensing, and optical detection.

A microcontroller running a digital control algorithm is used to regulate a physical plant, such as a motor speed or a temperature loop, and students tune the controller on hardware and compare its response to the simulation from lecture. Data logging and real-time plotting are used to diagnose steady-state error and oscillation caused by sampling rate or quantization. Laboratory companion to EENG-3065.

Continuous-time control designs are adapted for implementation on a microcontroller here, covering sampling rate selection, discretization of a continuous controller, and the effects of quantization and computational delay on closed-loop stability. Proportional-integral-derivative controllers are implemented in fixed-point arithmetic and evaluated against the same performance metrics used for their continuous counterparts.
