The course bridges classical control theory and the realities of running a controller on limited embedded hardware.

Working with a small laboratory plasma source, students measure electron temperature and density using electrostatic probes and observe basic plasma phenomena such as sheath formation and wave propagation. Diagnostic techniques including optical emission spectroscopy are used to characterize discharge conditions, and results are compared to the theoretical models covered in lecture. Laboratory companion to EENG-3075. Cross-listed with NUCL-2055.

Ionized gases are described through single-particle motion in electric and magnetic fields, then through fluid and kinetic models that predict collective behavior such as Debye shielding, plasma oscillations, and wave propagation. Diagnostic techniques used to measure plasma parameters, including probes and spectroscopic methods, are covered alongside the theory they are meant to test. Applications span fusion confinement concepts, plasma processing, and space plasma phenomena. Cross-listed with NUCL-2050.

Numerical methods for engineering problems are implemented here: root finding, numerical integration, linear system solvers, and basic data analysis and visualization applied to scientific data sets. Students write programs that process experimental or simulated data, propagate measurement uncertainty, and generate plots suitable for a technical report. The course moves quickly through basic programming constructs to focus most of its time on applying them to quantitative problem solving.

Field and bench measurements here characterize how radio signals attenuate and fade over distance, comparing measured path loss to free-space and empirical propagation models covered in lecture. Students also measure multipath effects indoors using a network analyzer and relate the results to fading statistics. Laboratory companion to EENG-4015.

Radio signal behavior over real terrain and buildings is modeled beyond simple free-space propagation, covering reflection, diffraction, and scattering mechanisms and the empirical and statistical models used to predict path loss in practice. Multipath fading, shadowing, and Doppler spread are analyzed for their effect on link reliability. Link budget calculations tie the propagation models to overall system range and coverage planning.

Students design and simulate the dynamic logic and memory circuits introduced in lecture, laying out an SRAM cell or a dynamic gate and verifying its read and write margins through transistor-level simulation. A semester project integrates a small memory block or a low-power logic circuit and evaluates it against area, speed, and power targets. Laboratory companion to EENG-4025.

Static gate design from the earlier design course expands here into dynamic logic families, memory circuits including SRAM and DRAM cell structures, and clocking and timing issues such as clock skew and setup and hold margins. Low-power design techniques, including voltage scaling and clock gating, are introduced alongside their tradeoffs against speed and reliability. Students analyze and design circuits that go well beyond the static gates covered earlier.

A pulsed or Q-switched laser system is operated on the bench here, with students measuring pulse energy, duration, and beam quality and comparing results to the mode-locking and Q-switching theory covered in lecture. A characterization exercise records output power as a function of pump level to extract threshold and slope efficiency for the system under test. Laboratory companion to EENG-4035.

This course extends the fundamentals of laser operation into pulsed and high-power regimes, covering Q-switching, mode-locking, and gain-switching techniques used to generate short optical pulses. Nonlinear effects such as harmonic generation and their role in extending laser wavelength coverage are also examined. Design problems estimate pulse energy, peak power, and repetition rate for a specified laser configuration.

Microwave circuits built from solid-state devices are analyzed using scattering parameters, covering transistor amplifier design for gain and stability, oscillator topologies, and mixer circuits used in microwave transceivers. Impedance matching networks are designed graphically to meet gain, bandwidth, and noise-figure targets. Design examples work through a complete low-noise amplifier or oscillator from device selection to matching network layout.

Digital control design is developed from the z-transform through pulse transfer functions, covering discretization of continuous plants, digital compensator design, and stability analysis on the z-plane. State-space methods for digital controllers, including pole placement and observer design, extend the classical transform-based techniques covered earlier in the course. Design examples apply these methods to mechanical and electromechanical plants such as a positioning stage or a motor drive. Cross-listed with MECH-3015.

Digital integrated circuits are examined at the chip level here, covering interconnect resistance and capacitance modeling, signal integrity issues such as crosstalk and ground bounce, and the power distribution networks needed to deliver clean supply voltage across a large die. Input and output buffer design and electrostatic discharge protection are covered as the interface between a chip and the outside world. The course complements gate-level design courses by focusing on effects that only appear at full-chip scale.

The electro-optic effect, the change in a material's refractive index under an applied electric field, is developed from crystal symmetry arguments and applied to the design of optical modulators and switches built in semiconductor and electro-optic crystal platforms. Phase and amplitude modulation schemes are analyzed for bandwidth and drive-voltage requirements. The course treats electro-optic modulation as a distinct device class from the light-emitting and light-detecting devices covered in earlier optoelectronics courses.

Electromagnetic field quantities such as electric field strength, transmission-line standing-wave ratio, and waveguide propagation characteristics are measured here using a network analyzer and probe setups, with results compared to the analytical predictions from lecture. A final exercise characterizes a transmission-line or waveguide section and extracts its propagation constant from measured data. Laboratory companion to EENG-4065.

Maxwell's equations are applied in their full form here, covering wave propagation in lossy and lossless media, transmission lines, waveguides, and boundary-value problems solved for canonical geometries. Time-harmonic fields are treated with phasor notation throughout, connecting the vector calculus formulation to practical transmission-line and waveguide design. The course provides the field-theory foundation used by later courses in antennas, microwave circuits, and optics.

Teams design, build, and program a robotic mechanism, integrating motors, sensors, and a microcontroller into a working system that must complete a specified physical task, such as picking up an object or navigating an obstacle course. Iterative testing and mechanical rework are a core part of the course, with students expected to diagnose and fix hardware failures under time pressure. Laboratory companion to EENG-4075.

Robot design is approached from the mechanism up: actuator selection and sizing, gear trains, manipulator kinematics, and the structural and electromechanical tradeoffs involved in building a physical robot rather than simulating one. Forward and inverse kinematics are developed for simple serial-link arms and applied to trajectory planning for a manipulator. The course emphasizes the mechanical and electromechanical design decisions that precede the navigation and perception algorithms covered in a separate robotics course.

Patentability, novelty, and obviousness are introduced from an engineer's perspective, covering how to read a patent claim, search prior art, and document an invention disclosure in a way that supports a later patent application. Case studies drawn from electrical and electronic technologies illustrate how claims are drafted to cover a range of implementations. The course is designed for engineers who will work alongside intellectual property professionals rather than for those pursuing formal legal training.

Surface plasmon polaritons, the coupled oscillations of free electrons and light at a metal-dielectric interface, are developed from Maxwell's equations and used to explain field confinement below the diffraction limit. Applications covered include plasmonic waveguides, sensors that exploit the sensitivity of surface plasmon resonance to a local refractive index change, and enhanced light-matter interaction in nanostructured metals. Numerical examples estimate propagation length and confinement for representative metal-dielectric geometries.

Semiconductor device behavior is derived here from the drift-diffusion and continuity equations rather than the simplified models used in an earlier course, covering short-channel effects, velocity saturation, and other second-order behavior in modern field-effect transistors. Bipolar transistor high-frequency limitations and heterojunction devices are also examined. Students use numerical device simulation to explore behavior that lacks a convenient closed-form solution.

Fiber-reinforced composites are introduced through their constituent phases: reinforcing fibers such as glass and carbon, and polymer, metal, or ceramic matrices that bind them. Coverage includes laminate stacking sequences, basic micromechanics for predicting stiffness and strength, and common fabrication routes like hand layup, filament winding, and resin transfer molding. Case studies from aerospace and automotive panels illustrate how fiber orientation and matrix choice drive performance tradeoffs. Cross-listed with MATL-1010.

The lab pairs basic machine shop practice (mill, lathe, drill press, and hand tools) with measurement technique using calipers, micrometers, and dial indicators. Students fabricate a sequence of simple parts from engineering drawings, checking dimensions and tolerances against spec, and submit lab reports documenting process choices and results. Safety procedures and shop etiquette are enforced from the first session. Laboratory companion to MANU-1015.

An entry point to product design, covering engineering sketching, dimensioning, and basic tolerancing alongside an overview of core manufacturing processes such as casting, injection molding, and machining. Simple design-for-manufacture guidelines introduce how part geometry and material choice affect cost and producibility. Weekly design exercises build toward a small manufactured component completed in the paired laboratory.

Coverage spans the equipment and layout decisions behind moving materials through a factory or warehouse: conveyors, automated guided vehicles, forklifts, and storage racking. Students learn to size throughput requirements, lay out receiving and staging areas, and calculate basic queuing and buffer capacity for a production line. Case examples cover distribution centers and assembly plants alike.

Material selection is framed as a design decision: given a set of functional requirements, students use property charts and selection indices to weigh candidate metals, polymers, ceramics, and composites against cost, weight, and manufacturability. Short case studies trace historical material substitutions, such as aluminum for steel in automotive panels, to show how selection criteria shift with application. Cross-listed with MATL-4005.

Laboratory sessions pair mechanical testing (tensile, hardness, and impact) with failure analysis of fractured or corroded samples, building the evidence base for a term-long material selection project. Students benchmark candidate materials against a design brief, document test procedures and data in formal reports, and present a final material recommendation. Laboratory companion to MANU-1025. Cross-listed with MATL-3020.

Manufacturers face volatile input costs, and this course examines how futures, forwards, options, and swaps are used to hedge exposure to raw-material prices, energy costs, and currency movements. Students build hedge ratios for a commodity-exposed production plan, evaluate basis risk, and compare exchange-traded contracts against over-the-counter alternatives. Applications draw on metals, plastics resin, and energy markets relevant to a manufacturing supply chain.

Building on first-year shop skills, this lab moves to CNC milling and turning, with students programming toolpaths from CAD models and verifying dimensional accuracy against tolerance stacks. Teams assemble multi-part subsystems, troubleshoot fit and function issues, and document machining parameters and iteration history in structured reports. Laboratory companion to MANU-2015.

Design work advances to parametric CAD modeling, geometric dimensioning and tolerancing, and formal design-for-manufacture and design-for-assembly review. Process planning introduces CNC machining sequences and fixturing strategy for mid-complexity parts, with tolerance stack-up analysis used to catch fit problems before they reach the shop floor. A term project carries a component from concept sketch through a manufacturing-ready drawing package.

Numerical optimization techniques such as gradient-based search, genetic algorithms, and topology optimization are applied to structural and mechanical design problems with competing objectives like weight, stiffness, and cost. Students formulate design variables, constraints, and objective functions for case problems such as bracket redesign or truss layout, then solve them with optimization software. Cross-listed with MECH-3020.

Cyclic loading and its effect on mechanical components anchors this course: S-N curves, stress concentration factors, and mean-stress corrections are used to predict fatigue life for shafts, fasteners, and welded joints. Crack initiation and propagation are introduced through basic fracture mechanics, including crack growth rate models. Historical failures, from aircraft fuselages to bridge components, illustrate how design margins are set in practice. Cross-listed with MECH-3025.

Lean principles built around waste elimination and flow are applied across both factory floors and service operations. Tools covered include value stream mapping, kanban pull systems, 5S workplace organization, and single-minute exchange of die for reducing changeover time. Students map an existing process, identify non-value-added steps, and propose a redesigned workflow with supporting metrics.

Conventional machining processes such as turning, milling, drilling, and grinding are analyzed through cutting mechanics: chip formation, tool geometry, and the speeds and feeds that govern material removal rate. Tool wear mechanisms and their effect on surface finish and dimensional accuracy are covered alongside selection of cutting tool materials such as carbide and ceramic inserts. Cross-listed with MECH-3045.

Fabrication and assembly methods for ships and offshore structures are covered, including hull plate forming, block construction sequencing, and welding procedures suited to marine-grade steel. Corrosion protection strategies such as cathodic protection and coating systems address the demands of a saltwater environment. Case studies examine how large sub-assemblies are built in modules and joined at final erection.

Coordination between a factory floor and its supply base is the focus, covering production planning basics, inventory positioning, and supplier lead-time management. Students calculate operational metrics such as overall equipment effectiveness and throughput, then use them to diagnose bottlenecks in a simplified multi-stage production system. Coordination mechanisms between purchasing, production, and logistics functions are examined through case scenarios.

Statistical methods for monitoring and improving process quality open with control charts: X-bar and R charts, p-charts, and the rules used to detect an out-of-control process. Process capability indices such as Cp and Cpk quantify how well a process meets specification limits, and acceptance sampling plans are introduced for incoming inspection. Worked examples draw on measurement data from machined parts and assembly lines. Cross-listed with MECH-2070.

Design work matures toward production readiness: students develop a manufacturing process plan for a multi-part assembly, estimate unit cost across candidate processes, and specify tooling requirements for a target production volume. Simulation tools check assembly tolerances and manufacturability before committing to hard tooling. The course bridges the single-part focus of earlier design courses with the system-level view needed for the capstone.

A team-based capstone carries a product from an initial concept through to a manufactured working prototype. Teams define requirements, iterate through concept selection and detailed design, and manage a build schedule that accounts for supplier lead times and shop availability. The term concludes with a functional prototype demonstration and a written design history documenting decisions and tradeoffs made along the way.

Design-for-manufacture rules are examined process by process: draft angles and wall thickness for injection molding, bend allowances and minimum flange lengths for sheet metal, and parting-line placement for casting. Students redesign a supplied part to reduce cycle time or scrap rate under a named manufacturing process, then justify the cost impact of each change. Cross-listed with MECH-2050.

Location decisions for manufacturing capacity are analyzed against labor cost, logistics distance, tariff exposure, and quality risk across regions. Case studies of multinational producers illustrate tradeoffs between offshoring, nearshoring, and reshoring, including the hidden costs of extended supply chains such as inventory buffers and quality escapes. Students build a landed-cost comparison for a candidate product across two or more manufacturing locations. Cross-listed with MECH-4020.

Factory-level design decisions are the subject: line balancing, cellular versus job-shop layout, and capacity planning for a target production rate. Discrete-event simulation models are built to test proposed layouts against throughput and work-in-process targets before committing to a floor plan. A term project designs a complete production system for a specified product and volume.

Manufacturing lines are modeled as networks of workstations, buffers, and material flows, and the course covers throughput analysis, bottleneck identification, and scheduling techniques used to improve production system performance. Queueing and simulation models are applied to case studies such as a circuit-board assembly line or an electronics test station. Students build a simplified simulation of a production line and use it to evaluate proposed changes in staffing or buffer sizing. Cross-listed with EENG-3005.

Building past the control-chart foundation of introductory quality control, this course covers design of experiments for process optimization, multivariate and EWMA control charts for detecting subtle shifts, and regression-based methods for relating process inputs to output quality. The DMAIC framework structures a term-long improvement project on a real or simulated process. Emphasis falls on situations where single-variable charts miss interacting effects.

Automated manufacturing equipment is built from the integration of sensors, actuators, and embedded control, and this course covers PLC programming, servo motor control, and sensor selection for closed-loop feedback. Students design and program a control system for a small automated workcell, such as a pick-and-place station or a robotic dispensing arm, addressing timing, safety interlocks, and fault handling. Cross-listed with MECH-4015.

An independent study format lets a student pursue an open design problem under faculty supervision, beginning with a written proposal that scopes the problem, deliverables, and schedule. Work proceeds through concept development, analysis, and design iteration appropriate to the chosen topic, culminating in a final written report and an oral presentation to faculty. Cross-listed with MATL-4010.

A supervised project applies manufacturing engineering methods to a problem proposed by the student and approved by a faculty advisor, covering process selection, cost analysis, or system design as the topic requires. Progress is tracked through periodic check-ins, with a final written report and presentation summarizing methodology, results, and recommendations. Topics have ranged from process improvement studies at a specific facility to the design of a manufacturing cell for a new product line.

Production planning and inventory management are formalized through models such as economic order quantity, safety stock calculation, and material requirements planning. Students build a master production schedule from a forecasted demand pattern and translate it into a time-phased materials plan for a multi-level bill of materials. Forecasting error and its effect on inventory buffers is examined through sensitivity analysis.

Sequencing and scheduling problems are formulated for both job shop and flow shop environments, covering dispatching rules, critical ratio scheduling, and bottleneck-focused approaches such as drum-buffer-rope. Students compare heuristic scheduling rules against optimal solutions for small problem instances and evaluate tradeoffs between makespan, tardiness, and machine utilization. A term assignment schedules a multi-product production run under capacity constraints.

Facility location and network design decisions are modeled for distribution centers, warehouses, and plants serving a regional or national demand pattern. Students apply location-allocation models to site new facilities, evaluate transportation cost tradeoffs between centralized and decentralized networks, and size warehouse space against throughput requirements. Case problems draw on retail distribution and manufacturing supply networks.

A team project embeds students directly with an industrial partner's operations to study a live production or logistics problem on-site. Teams scope the problem with the partner, gather operational data, and develop process or system recommendations grounded in the partner's actual constraints. The term concludes with a written report and a presentation delivered to the partner organization.

Ceramic materials are introduced through their crystal structures, ionic and covalent bonding, and the processing routes used to form dense parts, including powder pressing, sintering, and firing. Mechanical behavior emphasizes brittle fracture and the flaw sensitivity that distinguishes ceramics from metals, alongside thermal properties relevant to refractory and electronic applications. Examples range from structural alumina components to piezoelectric ceramics.

Fiber-reinforced composites are introduced through their constituent phases: reinforcing fibers such as glass and carbon, and polymer, metal, or ceramic matrices that bind them. Coverage includes laminate stacking sequences, basic micromechanics for predicting stiffness and strength, and common fabrication routes like hand layup, filament winding, and resin transfer molding. Case studies from aerospace and automotive panels illustrate how fiber orientation and matrix choice drive performance tradeoffs. Cross-listed with MANU-1005.

Hands-on sessions cover sample preparation, mounting, and coating techniques, followed by operation of a scanning electron microscope to capture and interpret micrographs of metal, ceramic, and polymer specimens. Basic diffraction patterns are collected and indexed to identify crystal structure. Each session produces a written report pairing imaging results with microstructural interpretation. Laboratory companion to MATL-1020.

The physics of electron-sample interaction underlies this introduction to electron microscopy, covering electron generation, lens systems, and imaging modes such as secondary electron, backscattered electron, and diffraction contrast. Resolution limits and specimen preparation constraints are compared across scanning and transmission instruments. The course builds the theoretical grounding for the paired laboratory's hands-on imaging work.

A broad survey introduces the four major materials classes (metals, polymers, ceramics, and composites) alongside the manufacturing processes commonly paired with each, such as casting for metals and injection molding for polymers. Basic property concepts, including strength, stiffness, and ductility, are related to atomic and molecular structure at a qualitative level. The course sets up the material and process vocabulary used throughout both the Materials Science and Manufacturing programs.

Covers the physical behavior of polymeric materials: chain conformation and molecular weight distribution, glass transition and crystallization, viscoelasticity, and the rheological measurements used to characterize melt and solution behavior. Problem sets connect molecular structure to bulk mechanical and thermal properties observed in processing. The course serves both chemical engineering and materials students, reflected in its dual listing. Cross-listed with CHEM-3015.

Material properties are derived from underlying physics: atomic bonding types, crystal structure, and electron band theory explain why some solids conduct electricity and others insulate. Thermal and magnetic properties, including heat capacity and basic ferromagnetism, are connected back to the same structural and electronic framework. Problem sets emphasize quantitative prediction of property trends across material families.

Structure-property relationships across metals, ceramics, and polymers are developed through mechanical testing, phase diagrams, and the microstructural features that control strength and toughness, including grain size, phase fraction, and defect density. Students interpret binary phase diagrams to predict microstructure from processing history and relate that microstructure to measured mechanical properties. The course applies these relationships to selecting materials for representative engineering components.

Diffusion and transport processes that govern materials processing are analyzed through Fick's laws, Arrhenius-type rate expressions, and time-temperature-transformation behavior. Applications include predicting carburizing depth in heat-treated steel, solidification rate effects on grain structure, and diffusion-controlled phase transformations. Problem sets require solving transport equations under specified boundary conditions relevant to processing operations.

Thermodynamic concepts such as Gibbs free energy, chemical potential, and phase equilibria are applied to materials systems to predict which phases are stable under given temperature and composition conditions. Reaction equilibria and basic electrochemistry extend the framework to corrosion behavior and oxidation of metals. Students construct and interpret binary phase diagrams from thermodynamic data.

Advanced characterization techniques extend beyond basic imaging to quantify composition and crystal structure: X-ray diffraction for phase identification, energy-dispersive spectroscopy for elemental analysis, and surface-sensitive methods for thin films and coatings. Students interpret diffraction patterns and spectra to solve materials identification problems drawn from failure analysis and quality control contexts. The course builds toward the hands-on instrument time in the paired laboratory.

Laboratory sessions put students on X-ray diffractometers and spectroscopy instruments to collect data on unknown material samples, then walk through pattern matching and quantitative analysis to identify phases and composition. Each session culminates in a written report defending an identification against the collected data. Instrument calibration and sample preparation practices are emphasized throughout. Laboratory companion to MATL-2030.

Metallic alloys are examined through the phase transformations and strengthening mechanisms that define their mechanical behavior: precipitation hardening, solid solution strengthening, grain refinement, and martensitic transformation in steels. Heat treatment schedules are designed and predicted using time-temperature-transformation and continuous-cooling-transformation diagrams for specific alloy systems. Case studies cover aluminum aerospace alloys and hardened tool steels.

Polymer chain architecture, molecular weight distribution, and crystallinity are connected to processing behavior across thermoplastics, thermosets, and elastomers. Processing methods such as extrusion, injection molding, and compression molding are examined alongside the viscoelastic response that distinguishes polymers from metals and ceramics, including creep, stress relaxation, and rate-dependent stiffness. Applications span commodity packaging plastics to engineering polymers used in structural components.

Laboratory sessions pair mechanical testing (tensile, hardness, and impact) with failure analysis of fractured or corroded samples, building the evidence base for a term-long material selection project. Students benchmark candidate materials against a design brief, document test procedures and data in formal reports, and present a final material recommendation. Laboratory companion to MATL-4005. Cross-listed with MANU-1030.

Short case studies trace historical material substitutions, such as aluminum for steel in automotive panels, to show how selection criteria shift with application. Cross-listed with MANU-1025.

An independent study format lets a student pursue an open design problem under faculty supervision, beginning with a written proposal that scopes the problem, deliverables, and schedule. Work proceeds through concept development, analysis, and design iteration appropriate to the chosen topic, culminating in a final written report and an oral presentation to faculty. Cross-listed with MANU-4010.

Newtonian mechanics of particles and rigid bodies grounds this course, covering position, velocity, and acceleration in rotating and translating reference frames. Students apply force-mass-acceleration and work-energy methods to problems in linkages, gears, and simple mechanisms, then extend the same tools to impulse and momentum. Rigid body rotation about fixed axes and general plane motion round out the semester's problem sets.

Free and forced response of single degree-of-freedom oscillators opens the course, with natural frequency, damping ratio, and resonance developed from spring-mass-damper models. Coverage extends to multi-degree-of-freedom systems, normal modes, and vibration isolation for rotating machinery. Problem sets emphasize predicting amplitude and frequency response from a system's physical parameters.

Truss and beam elements introduce the finite element method, with stiffness matrix assembly, boundary conditions, and solution of simple structural problems worked by hand before moving to software. Students compare mesh refinement choices and interpret displacement and stress output against known analytical solutions. The course builds intuition for where the method can mislead as well as where it helps.

Stress, strain, and the relationship between them under Hooke's law form the foundation of this course, applied first to axially loaded bars and then to circular shafts under torsion. Students compute deformation, factor of safety, and stress concentration in simple structural members. The course sets up the vocabulary and free body methods used throughout later mechanics coursework.

course_title: Modeling and Control of Dynamic Systems
course_desc: Differential equation models of mechanical, electrical, and electromechanical systems are converted into transfer functions and block diagrams as the starting point for this course. Students analyze first and second order system response to step and frequency inputs, then design basic proportional and PID feedback controllers. Root locus and Bode plot techniques are introduced as tools for predicting closed loop stability.

The first and second laws of thermodynamics anchor this course, developed through property tables, the ideal gas model, and control volume energy balances. Students evaluate work and heat transfer in closed and open systems, then apply the concepts to simple power and refrigeration cycles. Entropy generation and the limits it places on cycle efficiency close out the semester.

Electrochemical fundamentals of lithium-ion and related battery chemistries open this course, covering cell voltage, capacity, and internal resistance. Students model state of charge and state of health estimation algorithms and examine battery management system architectures for charge balancing and thermal protection. Case studies cover failure modes such as thermal runaway and degradation over repeated cycling.

Blood flow through arteries, veins, and capillary beds is modeled using non-Newtonian viscosity relationships suited to biological tissue, with pulsatile flow and vessel compliance treated alongside classical fluid mechanics. Students also examine respiratory airflow through the branching airway tree and the fluid dynamics of implanted and external biomedical devices such as stents, valves, and dialysis equipment. Problem sets connect physiological measurements to fluid mechanical models of disease and device performance.

Hertzian theory of elastic contact between curved surfaces opens the course, developed to predict contact area, pressure distribution, and subsurface stress. Students extend the analysis to friction, adhesion, and rolling contact, then apply it to wear prediction in bearings, gears, and cams. The course closes with an introduction to contact fatigue and surface failure mechanisms.

Design-for-manufacture rules are examined process by process: draft angles and wall thickness for injection molding, bend allowances and minimum flange lengths for sheet metal, and parting-line placement for casting. Students redesign a supplied part to reduce cycle time or scrap rate under a named manufacturing process, then justify the cost impact of each change. Cross-listed with MANU-3015.

Fluid statics and the control volume forms of mass, momentum, and energy conservation open this introduction to fluid mechanics, applied to problems in pipes, tanks, and open channels. Students use Bernoulli's equation and dimensional analysis to size simple flow systems and estimate friction losses in laminar and turbulent pipe flow. Lecture problems draw on manometry, flow measurement devices, and basic pump and turbine performance.

Elastic and plastic deformation of engineering metals and polymers is examined through stress-strain testing, yield criteria, and strain hardening models. Students study fatigue crack initiation and growth, creep at elevated temperature, and fracture mechanics parameters used to predict failure. Case studies connect microstructure to macroscopic mechanical response across a range of material classes.

Production line layout and process selection anchor this course, covering how batch size, tolerance requirements, and equipment capability shape a manufacturing system's design. Students apply line balancing, capacity planning, and material handling analysis to compare alternative factory layouts, then evaluate automation and robotics tradeoffs for a target production volume. Quality control methods, including statistical process control and inspection planning, are integrated into the design decisions throughout.

Statistical methods for monitoring and improving process quality open with control charts: X-bar and R charts, p-charts, and the rules used to detect an out-of-control process. Process capability indices such as Cp and Cpk quantify how well a process meets specification limits, and acceptance sampling plans are introduced for incoming inspection. Worked examples draw on measurement data from machined parts and assembly lines. Cross-listed with MANU-2050.

Bending, shear, and deflection of beams under distributed and concentrated loads extend the axial and torsional analysis introduced in earlier coursework. Students construct shear and moment diagrams, compute deflections by integration and superposition, and evaluate buckling of columns under compressive load. Combined loading problems and Mohr's circle for plane stress bring the semester's methods together for design against yield and instability.

Turbulence closure models, including eddy viscosity and Reynolds-averaged formulations, are developed alongside compressible gas dynamics for this advanced treatment of fluid flow. Students derive and apply the governing equations for shock waves, expansion fans, and choked flow in nozzles, then extend viscous flow theory to separated and three-dimensional boundary layers. The course is problem-set intensive, drawing on research-level fluid mechanics literature.

Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations replace the vector Newtonian methods of introductory dynamics, providing a systematic route to the equations of motion for constrained multibody systems. Students derive equations for robotic linkages, vehicle suspensions, and other multi-link mechanisms, then implement numerical integration schemes to simulate their time response. Generalized coordinates, virtual work, and Lagrange multipliers for constraints are recurring tools throughout.

Digital control design is developed from the z-transform through pulse transfer functions, covering discretization of continuous plants, digital compensator design, and stability analysis on the z-plane. State-space methods for digital controllers, including pole placement and observer design, extend the classical transform-based techniques covered earlier in the course. Design examples apply these methods to mechanical and electromechanical plants such as a positioning stage or a motor drive. Cross-listed with EENG-4045.

Numerical optimization techniques such as gradient-based search, genetic algorithms, and topology optimization are applied to structural and mechanical design problems with competing objectives like weight, stiffness, and cost. Students formulate design variables, constraints, and objective functions for case problems such as bracket redesign or truss layout, then solve them with optimization software. Cross-listed with MANU-2020.

Cyclic loading and its effect on mechanical components anchors this course: S-N curves, stress concentration factors, and mean-stress corrections are used to predict fatigue life for shafts, fasteners, and welded joints. Crack initiation and propagation are introduced through basic fracture mechanics, including crack growth rate models. Historical failures, from aircraft fuselages to bridge components, illustrate how design margins are set in practice. Cross-listed with MANU-2025.

The Navier-Stokes equations are derived and solved for a set of classical exact solutions before the course turns to boundary layer theory and its role in drag prediction. Students analyze laminar to turbulent transition, separation, and wake formation over immersed bodies such as airfoils and cylinders. External flow problems involving lift and drag coefficients connect the theory to vehicle and structure design.

Conduction, convection, and radiation are treated as a unified set of energy transport mechanisms, beginning with steady and transient conduction in one and two dimensional geometries. Students size fins and extended surfaces, apply correlations for forced and natural convection, and compute radiative exchange between surfaces of varying geometry and emissivity. The course closes with heat exchanger analysis using the log mean temperature difference and effectiveness-NTU methods.

State-space representation of linear time-invariant systems is developed from first principles, with matrix exponential solutions used to characterize free and forced response. Students evaluate controllability and observability using rank tests and design state feedback and observer gains by pole placement. Lyapunov methods for stability analysis and an introduction to optimal control close out the course.

Conventional machining processes such as turning, milling, drilling, and grinding are analyzed through cutting mechanics: chip formation, tool geometry, and the speeds and feeds that govern material removal rate. Tool wear mechanisms and their effect on surface finish and dimensional accuracy are covered alongside selection of cutting tool materials such as carbide and ceramic inserts. Cross-listed with MANU-2035.

Ordinary and partial differential equations that arise in mechanical engineering problems are solved using series solutions, separation of variables, and Laplace transform methods. Students apply linear algebra and matrix methods to coupled systems of equations, then use numerical techniques including finite differences to approximate solutions that resist closed form treatment. Applications are drawn from vibration, heat conduction, and structural problems covered elsewhere in the curriculum.

Life-cycle assessment quantifies the environmental impact of a product from raw material extraction through manufacturing, use, and disposal, forming the analytical core of this course. Students compare material and process alternatives for embodied energy, carbon footprint, and recyclability, then apply design for disassembly and design for energy efficiency principles to a term project. Regulatory drivers and eco-labeling standards are discussed alongside the technical methods.

Renewable generation technologies including solar photovoltaic, wind, and geothermal are evaluated for capacity factor, levelized cost, and grid integration challenges. Students design energy storage strategies combining batteries, pumped hydro, and thermal storage to firm intermittent generation, and model demand response and microgrid architectures. The course culminates in a techno-economic analysis of a proposed energy system.

Combustion chemistry and in-cylinder thermodynamics are developed for spark-ignition and compression-ignition engines, with emphasis on knock, ignition delay, and heat release rate. Students model emissions formation for nitrogen oxides, particulates, and unburned hydrocarbons, and evaluate aftertreatment and combustion control strategies for meeting emissions standards. Performance optimization problems cover boosting, variable valve timing, and fuel injection strategy.

Students design and program a control system for a small automated workcell, such as a pick-and-place station or a robotic dispensing arm, addressing timing, safety interlocks, and fault handling. Cross-listed with MANU-4005.

Case studies of multinational producers illustrate tradeoffs between offshoring, nearshoring, and reshoring, including the hidden costs of extended supply chains such as inventory buffers and quality escapes. Students build a landed-cost comparison for a candidate product across two or more manufacturing locations. Cross-listed with MANU-3020.

Powertrain architectures spanning series, parallel, and power-split hybrid configurations are compared for efficiency, packaging, and cost. Students size electric motors and battery packs against drive cycle requirements and design energy management strategies that split torque demand between the combustion engine and electric drive. Regenerative braking, engine start-stop control, and thermal management of the electric powertrain are covered as integrated design problems.

course_title: Special Topics in Mechanical Engineering Laboratory
course_desc: Experiments in this laboratory follow the rotating topic of its companion lecture, giving students hands-on apparatus time tied to that semester's subject matter. Students design test procedures, take instrumented measurements, and analyze uncertainty before writing formal laboratory reports. Equipment and measurement techniques vary by offering but consistently emphasize experimental method over any single topic area. Laboratory companion to MECH-4035.

Topics in this course rotate by offering and are announced in advance, drawing on emerging areas of mechanical engineering such as soft robotics, additive manufacturing process design, or biomechanical tissue modeling. Each offering is organized around a focused set of readings, problem sets, and a term project appropriate to the topic. The course allows the department to bring current research areas into the senior curriculum.

course_title: Special Topics in Mechanical Engineering II
course_desc: A second rotating special topics offering, this course covers subjects such as autonomous vehicle mechanical systems, tribology and surface engineering, or micro and nanoscale mechanical devices depending on the semester. Students work through topic-specific readings and a substantial project or paper that applies course concepts to an open problem. Because the subject changes each offering, the course may be repeated for credit as new topics are announced.

course_title: Computational Fluid Dynamics for Nuclear Applications
course_desc: Mesh generation and discretization of the governing flow equations introduce students to computational fluid dynamics as applied to nuclear reactor components such as coolant channels and fuel assemblies. Students set up and run simulations using standard turbulence models, then compare predicted velocity and temperature fields against benchmark data. The course emphasizes correct problem setup and result verification over the underlying numerical theory.

Image reconstruction algorithms for radiation detection systems form the focus of this course, covering projection data, back-projection, and iterative reconstruction methods. Students simulate detector response and reconstruct images from simulated and measured data using tomographic techniques common to medical and industrial imaging. Noise, resolution, and artifact sources are analyzed as limits on reconstructed image quality.

Coolant flow through reactor core channels is the organizing problem of this course, covering single-phase pressure drop, flow distribution among parallel channels, and the onset of boiling in two-phase conditions. Students apply mass, momentum, and energy balances to simplified core and heat exchanger geometries to predict coolant temperature and pressure profiles. The course builds the fluid mechanics foundation needed for later reactor thermal-hydraulics and safety analysis coursework.

course_title: Fundamentals of Nuclear Engineering and Radiological Sciences
course_desc: Nuclear reactions, radioactive decay, and the interaction of radiation with matter are introduced as the shared foundation for nuclear engineering and radiological science. Students calculate activity, half-life, and basic radiation dose, and survey reactor concepts alongside medical and industrial uses of radiation. The course establishes vocabulary and calculation methods used throughout the rest of the nuclear engineering curriculum.

Fission physics, the nuclear fuel cycle, and the major reactor types in commercial use are surveyed in this broad overview of the nuclear engineering field. Students trace uranium from mining through enrichment, fuel fabrication, reactor use, and waste management, and examine the regulatory and safety framework governing each stage. The course is oriented toward giving incoming majors a map of the discipline before they specialize.

course_title: Nuclear Core Design and Analysis I
course_desc: Fuel assembly geometry, enrichment distribution, and control rod placement are examined as design variables that determine a reactor core's neutron economy and power distribution. Students calculate power peaking factors and thermal margins against safety limits, and evaluate how core loading patterns affect fuel cycle length. The course introduces the design tradeoffs that core designers balance across successive fuel cycles.

Students operate scintillation and semiconductor radiation detectors in this laboratory, calibrating energy response and characterizing counting statistics against theoretical distributions. Weekly experiments cover pulse height analysis, dead time correction, and background subtraction using standard nuclear instrumentation electronics. Each experiment concludes with a written report presenting measured data alongside its statistical uncertainty. Laboratory companion to NUCL-1040.

Scintillation, semiconductor, and gas-filled detectors are compared for their response to radiation, energy resolution, and appropriate applications. Students study the electronics chain from preamplifier through pulse height analysis, and apply counting statistics to distinguish real signal from background and detector noise. Signal processing techniques for both pulse counting and spectroscopic measurement are covered.

Physical principles behind gamma camera, computed tomography, and positron emission imaging are developed from the interaction of radiation with detector and tissue material. Students trace the path from photon emission through detection to reconstructed image, comparing spatial resolution and sensitivity tradeoffs across modalities. The course sets up the physics used in later imaging and medical physics coursework.

Practical measurement techniques for gamma spectroscopy, alpha and beta counting, and neutron detection are developed for use in laboratory and field settings. Students calibrate instruments against certified sources, apply efficiency and geometry corrections, and evaluate measurement uncertainty for a range of detector types. Case studies cover environmental monitoring, contamination surveys, and material assay problems.

This laboratory puts the measurement techniques of its companion lecture into practice, with students calibrating detectors, counting certified sources, and performing efficiency and geometry corrections on their own data. Experiments cover gamma spectroscopy, alpha and beta counting, and simple neutron detection setups. Each session produces a written report documenting procedure, results, and measurement uncertainty. Laboratory companion to NUCL-2005.

Hands-on exercises in this laboratory demonstrate radiation applications in non-destructive testing, tracer studies, and sterilization dosimetry using departmental sources and equipment. Students plan and execute experiments, then interpret results in light of the application's practical constraints, such as dose limits or detection sensitivity. Written reports document experimental method, data, and interpretation for each application studied. Laboratory companion to NUCL-2020.

Industrial, medical, and research uses of radiation are surveyed, including non-destructive testing of materials, radiotracer studies, food and equipment sterilization, and well logging. Students evaluate the physical and practical constraints that shape each application, such as required penetration depth, dose limits, and detection sensitivity. The course connects the physics of radiation interaction to real deployment decisions across industries.

Magnetic confinement concepts, including the tokamak and stellarator configurations, are examined alongside the engineering challenges of sustaining a burning plasma. Students study first-wall and blanket materials, tritium breeding, and the heat removal systems required to handle fusion power densities. The course addresses the specific engineering problems that separate fusion reactor design from fission reactor practice.

course_title: Nuclear Engineering and Radiological Sciences II
course_desc: Building on the introductory survey, this course develops quantitative dose calculation methods, shielding fundamentals, and reactor physics concepts in greater depth. Students compute effective dose from mixed radiation fields and apply attenuation calculations to simple shielding geometries. The course bridges the department's introductory sequence and its more specialized upper-level coursework.

Point kinetics equations describe how reactor power responds to changes in reactivity, and form the analytical center of this course. Students work through delayed neutron effects, reactivity feedback from temperature and void changes, and transient response to control rod motion or reactivity insertion accidents. Numerical solution of the kinetics equations is used throughout to predict power excursions and their time constants.

Fuel pellet fabrication, cladding materials, and the fuel-cladding chemical interactions that develop over a fuel rod's life are the technical core of this course. Students track fuel performance through burnup, fission gas release, and dimensional changes, and evaluate fuel cycle chemistry for both uranium oxide and advanced fuel forms. The course connects fuel behavior to the operating limits imposed on reactor cores.

Kinetic theory of plasmas extends the fluid-like descriptions used in introductory treatments, developing the Vlasov equation and its role in describing collisionless plasma behavior. Students analyze plasma waves, instabilities, and Landau damping, then apply the theory to confinement and heating problems relevant to fusion devices. The course assumes familiarity with basic plasma concepts and moves quickly into more advanced kinetic and wave phenomena.

Ionized gases are described through single-particle motion in electric and magnetic fields, then through fluid and kinetic models that predict collective behavior such as Debye shielding, plasma oscillations, and wave propagation. Diagnostic techniques used to measure plasma parameters, including probes and spectroscopic methods, are covered alongside the theory they are meant to test. Applications span fusion confinement concepts, plasma processing, and space plasma phenomena. Cross-listed with EENG-3075.

Working with a small laboratory plasma source, students measure electron temperature and density using electrostatic probes and observe basic plasma phenomena such as sheath formation and wave propagation. Diagnostic techniques including optical emission spectroscopy are used to characterize discharge conditions, and results are compared to the theoretical models covered in lecture. Laboratory companion to NUCL-2050. Cross-listed with EENG-3070.

Radiation protection principles are applied specifically to medical settings in this course, covering dose limits for patients, staff, and the public in diagnostic and therapeutic environments. Students design shielding and room layouts for imaging suites and treatment areas, and evaluate regulatory compliance requirements for medical radiation facilities. Case studies address quality assurance programs and incident reporting practices in clinical radiation use.

Commercial reactor types, including pressurized water, boiling water, and advanced designs, are compared for their core configuration, coolant system, and safety systems. Students analyze plant-level thermodynamic cycles, balance of plant systems, and the operational characteristics that distinguish each reactor type. The course connects reactor physics and thermal-hydraulics concepts to full power plant design and operation.

Building on earlier instrumentation coursework, this course develops advanced spectroscopy and neutron detection methods used in research and nuclear security applications. Students apply coincidence counting, pulse shape discrimination, and advanced calibration techniques to distinguish signal sources in complex radiation fields. Data analysis methods for extracting isotopic and quantitative information from measured spectra are emphasized throughout.

Engineering applications of plasma outside the fusion context are the focus here, including plasma processing for semiconductor fabrication, plasma sources for surface treatment, and industrial plasma torches. Students design and characterize plasma generation systems, covering power coupling, electrode design, and diagnostic measurement of plasma parameters. The course emphasizes applied plasma engineering rather than the confinement physics covered in fusion-focused coursework.

course_title: Research in Nuclear Engineering and Radiological Sciences
course_desc: Students undertake a supervised research project in nuclear engineering or radiological sciences under a faculty advisor's direction, beginning with a written proposal defining scope and methods. Work proceeds through data collection or analysis appropriate to the chosen topic, culminating in a written report and a presentation of findings to the sponsoring research group. The course structure varies by project but consistently requires a proposal, a final report, and a presentation.

course_title: Radiation Safety and Medical Physics Practicum
course_desc: This practicum places students in a clinical or radiation safety office setting under professional supervision, observing and assisting with duties such as survey work, dosimetry checks, and safety program administration. Students keep a log of practicum activities and complete a written report connecting observed practice to radiation safety and medical physics principles. A final presentation summarizes the practicum experience and its key lessons for the sponsoring program.

Treatment planning for external beam and brachytherapy is developed from the physics of linear accelerators and sealed radioactive sources used in cancer therapy. Students calculate dose distributions using treatment planning algorithms and evaluate plan quality against target coverage and organ-at-risk constraints. Quality assurance procedures for therapy equipment round out the course's clinical physics content.

Attenuation and buildup factor calculations for gamma rays and neutrons form the quantitative core of this course, applied to shield design for reactors, medical facilities, and radioactive material storage. Students select shielding materials and thicknesses to meet dose limits at specified distances, accounting for source geometry and scattered radiation. The course culminates in a shielding design project evaluated against regulatory dose criteria.

Advanced dosimetry calculations, including cavity theory and dose conversion coefficients, extend the measurement and shielding concepts developed earlier in the curriculum. Students compute absorbed, equivalent, and effective dose for complex exposure scenarios and evaluate dosimeter response across radiation types and energies. As a senior capstone course, it draws together radiological physics principles from across the nuclear engineering sequence.
